opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a good question, and honestly my view has shifted over time.

When we started, vocabulary size felt like a fairly minor hyperparameter. You pick something around 32k, you train your BPE or SentencePiece model, and you move on. Over time it became clear that this "minor" choice has real consequences. If the vocabulary is larger, you compress the text better, so you fit more content into the same context window and spend less compute per unit of information. That matters a lot for multilingual data and for code, where a small vocabulary fragments everything into tiny pieces. So there's been a natural push toward bigger vocabularies, into the hundreds of thousands.

But you can't grow it forever. First, the embedding and output layers get expensive. At smaller model scales the softmax over a huge vocabulary eats a meaningful share of your parameters and compute. Second, you hit a long-tail problem. The more tokens you add, the rarer each new one is, so many of them are barely seen during training and end up with poorly learned representations. You get these weird under-trained tokens that can cause strange behavior. Third, there are diminishing returns on compression. Past a certain point, each extra token buys you very little.

So I don't think "just make the vocabulary bigger" is the long-term answer. Tokenization is still a bit of an embarrassing hack in the middle of an otherwise end-to-end learned system. It's a fixed, greedy, frequency-based preprocessing step that the model has no say in, and it causes real problems: the classic failures on character-level tasks, counting letters, arithmetic where numbers get split inconsistently, and unfairness across languages, where some languages cost three or four times more tokens to express the same thing.

Where I'd like to see things go, and where I think they will go eventually, is toward models that learn their own segmentation. Byte-level or character-level models with some hierarchical or dynamic patching, so the model decides how to chunk the input based on how predictable it is. You spend more compute where the text is hard and less where it's easy. There's been promising research in that direction, and the main obstacle has been efficiency at scale. Pure byte-level sequences are long, and attention cost is what it is.

My guess is that we'll keep using tokenizers pragmatically for a while, because they work and the whole infrastructure is built around them. In the longer run, I'd be surprised if we're still hand-designing vocabularies. Removing that last non-learned component feels like the natural direction, the same "let the model learn it" lesson that has played out everywhere else in deep learning.

r001.rationale: The response says large vocabularies can make the softmax costly, especially at smaller model scales, but does not suggest that larger models can accommodate them without substantial training impact.

r002.rationale: It proposes byte-level or character-level models with hierarchical or dynamic patching as a future direction.

r003.rationale: The response does not raise pixel-level decomposition as an approach to multimodal tokenization.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think about a lot, because tokenization is one of those parts of the stack that everyone kind of agrees is ugly, and yet nobody has really managed to get rid of it.

So first, on vocabulary size. We went from 32k with the first Llama to 128k with Llama 3, and there were real gains from that. You get better compression, so the same text costs fewer tokens, which means cheaper inference and effectively a longer context window for free. And it helps a lot for multilingual, because with a small vocabulary you're basically penalizing every language that isn't English, where a word that is one token in English becomes four or five tokens in Hindi or Thai.

But there's clearly a limit. The vocabulary is also your output layer, so as you grow it you're spending more and more parameters and compute on the embedding and unembedding matrices, and for a small model that quickly becomes a big fraction of the whole thing. And the other thing is that rare tokens get trained very little. If you have a million tokens, a lot of them will be seen a handful of times, and the model doesn't learn a good representation for them. So you get this long tail of under-trained tokens, which is where a lot of the weird behavior comes from, the glitch tokens and so on. So I don't think we go to a million tokens. I think somewhere in the range we are now, maybe a bit higher, is close to the sweet spot for text with the current approach.

Now, the longer-term question is whether we want tokenization at all. And my honest view is that BPE is a heuristic. It's a compression algorithm from the nineties that we bolted onto the front of the model because training on bytes was too expensive. It's not learned, it's not end-to-end, and it creates all these artifacts. The model can't count letters properly, it struggles with arithmetic because numbers are split in arbitrary ways, and it's brittle to typos and to any language or domain that the tokenizer wasn't fit on.

So the direction I find exciting is making tokenization learned and dynamic. Work like the Byte Latent Transformer, where you operate on bytes but group them into patches based on the entropy of the next byte, so you spend more compute where the text is hard to predict and less where it's easy. That's conceptually much more satisfying than a fixed vocabulary, because the model decides how to allocate compute rather than a preprocessing step. And it scales better to new languages, to code, to anything.

The challenge is efficiency. Tokenization is free at inference, and these learned approaches add some overhead. But I think this is the same story as many things in deep learning. The hand-crafted feature loses eventually. We removed hand-crafted features from vision, from speech, and the tokenizer is the last big hand-crafted feature in language models. So I'd bet that in a few years, the models we train are much closer to end-to-end on bytes, and the vocabulary question kind of disappears, because the model learns its own.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a tradeoff. If you make the vocabulary larger, you can represent more things with fewer tokens, so your sequences get shorter. But you’re also making the embedding table and the output layer larger, and you need enough data to learn useful representations for all those tokens. You can’t just keep adding every possible word or combination of words.

The more interesting question is whether tokenization should be a fixed preprocessing step at all. We decide in advance how to split the input, and then the model has to work with that decision. Ideally, I’d like the model to learn the level of representation it needs: sometimes a small unit, sometimes a much larger one.

Going directly to bytes is one possible direction, but then you have longer sequences, so you haven’t eliminated the cost—you’ve moved it. The challenge is to combine that flexibility with efficient computation. I think that’s more promising than simply growing the vocabulary indefinitely.

sol-6.1.text:
I think vocabulary size is a trade-off. If you make it larger, you can represent more text with fewer tokens, which is useful because sequence length is expensive. But you also make the embedding and output layers larger, and you have more tokens that appear rarely, so learning good representations for them becomes harder. You can’t just keep increasing the vocabulary forever and expect it to be better.

The more interesting question is whether tokenization should be a fixed preprocessing step at all. We choose these discrete units before training, and then the model has to work with that choice. Ideally, you would like the model to learn the useful units itself. Maybe it operates on bytes at the input, but internally learns to group them into something more efficient.

The challenge is doing that without paying the computational cost of treating every byte as a full token. So I would distinguish getting rid of a handcrafted tokenizer from getting rid of compression. I can imagine the first happening; you still need the second. The question is where that compression happens and whether it can be learned jointly with the model.
